summary.headline: A good renewable power business, but the price already counts on projects still being built
summary.text:
Vidullanka PLC (VLL.N0000 voting, VLL.X0000 non-voting) runs 76 MW of hydro, solar and biomass plants. Most of its profit comes from two Ugandan hydro plants paid in US dollars. It passes all four business tests: return on equity of 15–19% for five years, net debt 0.68x equity, a profit of over Rs 1bn for four years running, and a dividend paid every year.

Results are softening, though. Owners' profit for the half to September 2026 rose 13% to Rs 671mn, but only because of Rs 245mn of other income the report doesn't explain. The September quarter fell 58% as finance costs more than doubled. Net debt doubled to Rs 6.85bn in six months, borrowed for battery storage and new solar plants, and the interim dividend was cut to Rs 0.20.

At Rs 22.00 (CSE close, 18 November 2026) the share is 2.25x NAV of Rs 9.76 and about 15x trailing EPS. Five methods put fair value at about **Rs 8.88**. I'd buy at up to **Rs 7.54** and treat **Rs 6.66** or less as a strong buy. The market is already paying for projects that haven't earned anything yet. Category 2: watch list.

fullText:
VIDULLANKA PLC (VLL.N0000 voting, VLL.X0000 non-voting): long-term valuation, 2026-11-18 (redo)

SUMMARY
Vidullanka is a renewable power producer with 76 MW of hydro, solar and biomass ("dendro") plants in Sri Lanka, plus two hydro plants in Uganda that earn most of its profit. It passes all four business tests: return on equity of 15–19% for five years, net debt 0.68x equity, a profit of more than Rs 1bn for four years running, and cash flow that pays a dividend every year. At Rs 22.00 (voting, CSE close 18 November 2026), though, the share is 2.25x book value and about 15x trailing earnings. Five methods put fair value at about Rs 8.88. I'd buy at up to Rs 7.54 and treat Rs 6.66 or less as a strong buy. The price assumes the battery storage, wind and new solar projects will earn far more than the cost of capital. That may happen, but it isn't in the figures yet. Category 2: watch list.

WHAT CHANGED IN THIS REDO
Second redo on 18 November, from the saved record (no new reports). The whole-company DCF plus the joint ventures and projects is now saved in the model inputs, with the stakes as a fixed add-on of Rs 3.44 / 4.22 / 6.10 a share, so the "What if?" panel can move the DCF part too. The calculator reproduces the published Rs 3.41 / 9.26 / 19.05. Every assumption was rechecked; none changed, and the price is still Rs 22.00, so fair value stays Rs 8.88.

EARLIER THE SAME DAY (full redo)
This rebuilds the 17 November analysis from the same two reports, at the CSE close of Rs 22.00 instead of the Rs 22.10 last trade in the interim. The figures were rechecked against the statements and nothing needed correcting. The 2025 year-end share count (1,027.2mn) is now recorded. New sections: management and plans, shareholders, and the model inputs behind the "What if?" panel. P/E, P/B, residual income and dividend values now come from scripts/valuation.py. Its forward justified P/E (5.5 / 6.6 / 8.2x) is a little lower than the hand figures used before (5.8 / 6.9 / 8.7x). Residual income now fades ROE from 16% to each scenario's level. Bull dividend growth is now 8%, below the 8.9% the kept profit supports. Fair value moves from Rs 8.95 to Rs 8.88.

THE BUSINESS
- Overseas hydro (Muvumbe and Bukinda, 6.5 MW each, Uganda): revenue Rs 2.55bn and profit Rs 1.21bn in 2025/26, about three-quarters of group profit. The tariff is in US dollars: Bukinda earns Rs 31.13 (US$0.0957) a unit, with 15 years of contract left (p. 147). Muvumbe's remaining term isn't given. Profits sent home pay withholding tax (Rs 144.6mn in the half to September 2026).
- Local mini-hydro: revenue Rs 0.53bn and profit Rs 0.42bn. Several contracts have been renewed (Bambarabatuoya to 2036, Batathota to 2041, Gurugoda to 2044); Lower Kotmale has 8 years left.
- Solar: 21 MW added in 2025/26 through four projects, plus the Vavunathivu plants held through Solar Universe, an associate with WindForce. The 10 MW Ranna plant was due on the grid in September 2026; the interim doesn't confirm it.
- Dendro and plantation: Dehiattakandiya (51% joint venture). Medawachchiya, 6.6 MW, is under construction: Rs 1.3bn equity commitment, Rs 0.5bn put in, commissioning targeted for mid-2027/28.
- New lines: 49% of Storex, which is building twelve 10 MW / 40 MWh battery storage sites (Rs 2.2bn invested in the September quarter); 30% of the 10 MW Alankuda wind plant; the 50 MW Mullikulam wind tender (with the David Peiris Group); lowest bidder, with Skipper, for a Rs 5bn transmission line for the CEB; and a US$1.35mn mini-hydro build in Fiji.
- Buyers: the National System Operator (NSO, split out of the CEB) in Sri Lanka and UETCL in Uganda. The report mentions slower payments during the CEB's restructuring, and output curtailed by the grid: Rs 119mn of lost energy from March 2025 to September 2026.

LATEST RESULTS
Six months to 30 September 2026 (unaudited): revenue Rs 2.04bn (+6%), gross profit Rs 1.43bn (+2%), profit to owners Rs 671mn (+13%). The rise came from Rs 300mn of other income. The cash flow statement removes Rs 245mn of it as non-cash, and the report doesn't explain it. Finance costs more than doubled to Rs 357mn. The September quarter alone was weak: profit to owners Rs 131mn against Rs 311mn (−58%), with finance costs of Rs 210mn (+161%) and cost of sales up 28%. Overseas hydro revenue fell 12% in the half, while solar rose to Rs 408mn from Rs 92mn. EPS for the half is about Rs 0.65 on all 1,038mn shares. The report shows Rs 0.70 because it divides by 954mn shares (voting only, it seems), unlike the annual report, which counts both classes.
Balance sheet: net debt (borrowings and leases less cash) rose from Rs 3.36bn in March to Rs 6.85bn in September. Rs 1.96bn went on plant and Rs 1.89bn net into new projects, mainly Storex. NAV per share is Rs 9.76. The interim dividend was Rs 0.20 (Rs 0.35 a year earlier).
Year to March 2026 (audited): revenue Rs 3.83bn (Rs 5.42bn a year earlier, which included Rs 2.1bn from a finished engineering contract in Guyana). Profit after tax Rs 1.55bn (Rs 1.58bn), of which owners Rs 1.49bn; EPS Rs 1.45 (Rs 1.56). Generation 229 GWh (+15%), capacity 76 MW (51 MW). Dividends Rs 0.65 a share (Rs 1.70, of which Rs 1.20 was paid in shares).

MANAGEMENT AND PLANS
The Chairman and CEO describe 2025/26 as a year of rapid investment. Capacity rose 50%, Uganda carried profit, and the CEB's break-up slowed payments. Battery storage is now a core focus, with wind next, then a second dendro plant and growth in Africa. Promises against delivery so far: the Storex battery stake and Medawachchiya are funded and on track, and the Fiji contract was won. Ranna's connection isn't confirmed. The promised "healthy balance" between dividends and funding projects hasn't held this half: net debt doubled, finance costs rose 128%, and the interim dividend was cut.

SHAREHOLDERS
Directors and their families hold 71.6% of the voting shares. CEO Riyaz Sangani holds 23.5% across three accounts, Chairman Osman Kassim 13.7%, Sattar Kassim 10.7% and the Mathers about 18.5%. The public holds 28.4% (4,885 holders, up from 4,070 in March). Between March and September the Chairman's main account sold 7.1m shares (about 5% of it). Mr Sangani's own account added 3.75m and his NDB account fell 1.69m. Foss Ltd entered the top 20 with 7.6m, and Esanjo Capital dropped out. The non-voting class is led by Ms N. R. Mather (29.7%, unchanged).

REINVESTMENT AND GROWTH
2025/26 was a heavy build year. Capex booked was Rs 2.73bn (including Rs 1.64bn of solar plant for the four new projects and Rs 0.68bn of land) against depreciation of Rs 0.44bn, plus Rs 0.66bn into joint ventures and projects. That spending is mostly growth, to be judged on its return, not upkeep. Net debt rose by more than half the capex, so it was largely borrowed (the calculator flags this). The calculator gives a reinvestment rate of 198% of after-tax operating profit at a 16.6% return on capital: supported growth of 32.8%. That figure is inflated by one build year. I assume 3% / 6% / 9% for five years, well inside it, because each new project also needs new money. Long-run growth is 3 / 4 / 5%, below the 12.24% bond yield and WACC, with reinvestment of growth ÷ return on capital. It is kept modest because plant contracts are finite and some overseas plants are build-own-transfer.
Maintenance capex: the company gives no split. The calculator's range is Rs 1.43bn / 0.77bn / 0.44bn, but its top two figures are distorted by the build year (land and new solar plant in capex booked). For plants on long contracts, depreciation (about Rs 0.55bn a year now) is a fair base. I use bear Rs 0.75bn, base Rs 0.55bn and bull Rs 0.44bn, which is 0.8–1.4x depreciation; the bear case is slightly above the usual 1.3x, for safety.
Cash and dividend cover: FY2026 cash from operations was Rs 1.34bn, after Rs 0.93bn of tax paid and Rs 0.64bn more receivables. Dividends were Rs 0.75bn including minorities. On the calculator's base maintenance (Rs 0.77bn), that year's cash after maintenance (Rs 0.57bn) didn't cover the dividend; on depreciation-level upkeep it covers about 1.05x. In the half to September, cash from operations was Rs 0.58bn against Rs 0.28bn of depreciation and Rs 0.25bn of dividends paid. **The dividend is at risk** while debt-funded projects ramp up, which fits the interim cut.

REQUIRED RETURN
Cost of equity = risk-free 8.24% (12.24% 10-year bond less a 4.0% default spread) + beta 0.70 × (4.2% mature premium + 6.08% country premium) = 15.4%; bear 16.9%, bull 13.9%. The beta is provisional. It starts from Damodaran's global Green & Renewable Energy unlevered beta of 0.57 (a web-search figure, January 2026). His emerging-markets file couldn't be reached from this run either. Relevered at net debt of 0.30x market value with 25% tax, it gives 0.70. Only one local 5-year beta was found (0.28), so step 4 is incomplete. The result is inside the 12–22% range for CSE shares, at the low end because contracted power is steady. No extra premium is added for Uganda, although most of the profit comes from there. Cost of debt is 9.56% (interest paid ÷ average borrowings and leases, FY2026), 7.2% after tax. WACC is 13.5% (debt weight 23.1% at Rs 22.00); bear 14.7%, bull 12.3%.

VALUATION
Methods: a whole-company DCF of the consolidated plants (at WACC, less net debt) plus the joint ventures and project stakes; P/E; justified price to book; residual income; and a two-stage dividend model. Fair value weights each scenario's average 30/50/20.
- Whole-company DCF + joint ventures and projects: Rs 3.41 / 9.26 / 19.05 (weighted 9.46). The consolidated plants are valued as a whole company. Cash before interest after maintenance capex is Rs 1.10 / 1.48 / 1.80bn: after-tax operating profit of Rs 1.30 / 1.48 / 1.69bn (operating profit excluding joint ventures of Rs 1.85 / 2.05 / 2.25bn, after 30 / 28 / 25% tax), plus depreciation of about Rs 0.55bn, less maintenance. It grows 3% / 6% / 9% for five years, then 3 / 4 / 5%, less the reinvestment that growth needs at a 12 / 15 / 17% return on capital. Discounted at WACC of 14.7 / 13.5 / 12.3%, less net debt of Rs 6.85bn (30 September 2026), the calculator gives Rs −0.03 / 5.04 / 12.95 a share. Value after year 5 is 58% / 70% / 80%: the bull case is over the 75% flag, so most of it rests on the long run. Then add the joint ventures (Rs 2.43bn book) and project investments, mainly Storex (Rs 2.21bn at cost), less minorities (Rs 0.26bn): Rs 3.44 / 4.22 / 6.10 a share. That is 85% / 80% of book in the bear case, book in the base case, and 1.35x / 1.5x in the bull case. The start cash is above the calculator's operating-cash figure (Rs 0.19 / 0.85 / 1.17bn) because 2025/26 operating cash was held down by NSO payment delays and by tax on the previous year's higher profit.
- P/E method: Rs 6.37 / 8.92 / 12.29 (weighted 8.83). EPS for the year to March 2027 of Rs 1.15 / 1.35 / 1.50 times 5.5 / 6.6 / 8.2. That is the forward P/E justified at the cost of equity when growth is paid for (payout = 1 − growth ÷ ROE; ROE 14 / 16 / 17%, growth 4 / 5 / 6%). Base EPS is 10.6% below the Rs 1.51 run-rate (last 12 months; the latest quarter × 4 is only Rs 0.51). The run-rate includes Rs 0.245bn of unexplained other income, and finance costs have doubled on borrowing for projects that aren't earning yet; without the item the run-rate is about Rs 1.28.
- Justified price to book: Rs 7.57 / 10.32 / 13.59 (weighted 10.15): 0.78 / 1.06 / 1.39x the NAV of Rs 9.76. Rs 22.00 is 2.25x book, which would need a lasting ROE of about 28% at the base cost of equity.
- Residual income: Rs 7.61 / 10.47 / 14.10 (weighted 10.34). ROE moves from 16% to 14 / 16 / 17% over ten years, with 45% paid out. After that the excess return grows at 4 / 5 / 6%. ROE is close to the cost of equity, so little is added to book.
- Dividends (two-stage): Rs 3.60 / 5.59 / 8.63 (weighted 5.60). The 2026/27 dividend is Rs 0.50 / 0.60 / 0.70, growing 3 / 6 / 8% for five years, then 3 / 4 / 5%. This is the lowest method because more than half of profit is kept for new plants.
Averages: bear Rs 5.71, base Rs 8.91, bull Rs 13.53. Fair value Rs 8.88 (0.91x NAV). Buy price Rs 7.54 (15% below), strong buy Rs 6.66 (25% below).
Ratio checks: beta 0.70, cost of equity 15.4% and WACC 13.5% (below the cost of equity) are in range. Net debt/EBITDA is about 2.5x (trailing EBITDA about Rs 2.7bn, including the unexplained Rs 0.245bn), under 3x. Vidullanka also guarantees Rs 1.64bn of joint-venture and associate loans (p. 166). The P/Es (5.5–8.2x) and P/Bs (0.78–1.39x) are the justified figures, so they imply no more growth than is supported. The cost of debt (9.56%) is within the −4 / +8 point band around the bond yield.

WHY THE MARKET PAYS MORE
At Rs 22.00 the market values the company at about Rs 22.6bn plus Rs 6.85bn of net debt. Against trailing EBITDA of about Rs 2.7bn, that is about 9.3x after taking out the Rs 4.6bn of joint-venture and project stakes. Buyers are paying for the pipeline: battery storage at 12 sites, wind, more solar and the transmission line. If those earn well above the 13–15% cost of capital, the bull case rises. But most of them are still being built or bid for, and so far they have mainly brought higher debt and finance costs. The report also cites curtailment and lower solar tariffs as having hurt operations (p. 36). I value the new projects at cost (1.5x in the bull case) until they produce results.

BUY PLAN (500 shares)
200 shares up to Rs 7.54, 150 up to Rs 7.10, 150 up to Rs 6.66: average about Rs 7.14, total about Rs 3,570 (Rs 11,000 at Rs 22.00).
Realism: Rs 7.54 needs a fall of about 66%. The voting share traded at Rs 19.90–23.40 in the September quarter and Rs 12.90–31.00 in 2025/26, so it isn't likely soon. The non-voting share (Rs 19.10) is about 13% cheaper and has the same rights to profit, but no vote.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE VIEW
Higher: battery storage sites commissioned and earning, with tariffs known; Ranna, Medawachchiya and the wind projects running to budget; the NSO paying on time and curtailment ending; the Uganda contracts extended.
Lower: further profit drops like the September quarter; debt rising faster than new plants come on line; tariff cuts or more curtailment; poor rainfall in Uganda or Sri Lanka; the rupee strengthening against the dollar (lowering Ugandan profit in rupees); trouble at the joint ventures whose loans Vidullanka guarantees.

UNCERTAINTIES
- The Rs 245mn of "other income" in the half-year isn't explained in the interim report.
- The interim EPS uses 954mn shares, not the 1,038mn in issue; I've recomputed it.
